The snare drum is the first drum most players meet, and the one whose technique carries over to the rest of the section. It has a
shallow shell, a **batter head** on top that you hit, and a bottom head with a set of **snares** (wires) stretched across it that buzz
when the top head is struck. This page follows the percussion chapter of a teacher book (Kjos W74), in this site's own words. The
sticks, grips, strokes, head changing and tuning are on [the Percussion page](percussion.qmd).

## Set-up {#setup}

1. Take the stand out of its case, open the legs and tighten the leg lock. Make the stand level on the floor.
2. If the stand is in pieces, fit the top into the base. Set the height so the **top rim of the drum is a little below your waist**.
   Many snare stands are made for a drum set and sit too low for concert playing. If so, an extension tube is needed.
3. Open the support arms all the way and set their angle so the drum is level, or tilted a little.
4. Take the drum out of its case and lay it on the arms with the **snares facing the floor** and the release lever straight in front of
   you. The arms should hold it snugly (not over-tight) and must not touch the strainer, the snare head or the snares.
5. Adjust the snare tension knob until the sound is crisp and clear.
6. Put the music stand directly in front of the drum, just below eye level.

## Stick grip {#grip}

1. Bend your arm at the elbow so the forearm slopes slightly away from the floor.
2. Pick a stick and find the spot about **a third of the way from the butt**. Pinch it between the first joint of your index finger and
   the pad of your thumb. That is the **fulcrum**, the pivot point. The stick should feel tip-heavy, not evenly balanced. (Some
   players make the fulcrum with the middle finger instead of the index finger.)
3. Wrap the other fingers lightly round the stick so they touch it but stay relaxed. Leave a little gap between your thumb and index
   finger. The thumb points toward the tip. Turn your wrist so your palm faces down.
4. Do the same with the other hand so the two grips mirror each other. This is **matched grip**.

**Traditional grip** (the left hand only; the right hand is as above). Put the stick in the web between thumb and index finger,
about a third up from the butt, gripped just tightly enough to keep it there. Rest the shaft on the **ring finger** between its first and
second joints, with the little finger beside it, the other two fingers on top of the stick and the thumb resting lightly on the index
finger. A left-hand stroke comes from the forearm and wrist turning, as if turning a doorknob.

## Playing position {#position}

1. Stand behind the drum, feet comfortably apart, weight even, body free of tension.
2. Hold the sticks loosely with the forearms angled slightly downward, palms down, elbows level with the sides of the body but slightly
   away from them.
3. Put the stick tips together at about **90 degrees**.
4. Move toward the drum until the sticks are above the head a little off-centre and **1 to 2 inches** up. This is the ready position.
   Change the stand height if you need to. (A tip from the book: "air drum" on an imaginary drum first, then go to the real one and set
   the stand to match how you naturally stand.)

## First strokes {#first-strokes}

1. Raise the tip 8 to 12 inches above the head with your wrist, then drop it and let the stick **rebound** to where it began. That
   is a full stroke. Use a relaxed wrist motion, like bouncing a ball. Hit slightly off-centre, directly above the snares, and adjust
   until it sounds best.
2. To play again with the same hand, go straight into the down motion of the next stroke. To stop between strokes, let the stick
   bounce up to rest at 1-2 inches (a down stroke).
3. Change volume by changing the height the stick starts from. Starting lower is softer, there is less rebound, and the wrist does
   more of the work. At every volume aim for a **round, crisp** sound.

Where on the head? Just off-centre rings best. The edge is often good for soft passages. Dead centre is drier, which helps when a
passage needs lots of articulation.

### Snare drum checklist

- Standing up straight, weight on both feet, a good distance from the drum?
- Forearms at a slight angle to the floor?
- Sticks held correctly?
- Right and left strokes sounding the same?
- Striking the right place; sticks rebounding; good tone?

## Rim work, snares off and brushes {#techniques}

- **Playing on the rim.** Hit the rim with the shoulder or shaft of the stick, in either or both hands, for a wooden sound.
- **Rim shot.** A sharp "crack". *One hand:* a forceful stroke that hits the head with the tip and the rim with the shoulder or shaft
  at the same time; always loud, and good when rim shots fall among normal strokes. *Two hands:* lay the tip of one stick on the head,
  shaft held up at an angle, and hit that shaft with the shoulder or shaft of the other stick. It is easier and any volume, but the set-up
  means it can only be an isolated note.
- **Cross-stick** (also rim click or side stick). Lay a stick across the drum with its tip on the head and the butt over the rim. Using
  the tip as a pivot, lift with the index finger and thumb, then lower to the rim. The tip stays on the head the whole time. It
  combines the wooden sound of the rim with the drum's resonance.
- **Snares off.** The part tells you to throw off the release lever. The drum then sounds like a high-pitched tenor drum or tom when the
  batter head is struck. The way you play does not change.
- **Brushes.** Used a lot in jazz and show music, and for special effects on other instruments too. They are held with matched or
  traditional grip. For ordinary rhythms use the same strokes as with sticks, but there is less rebound, so the wrist has to supply it.
  For a smooth "swishing" or "stirring" sound, slide the wires of one brush (usually the left) round the head in steady circles or ovals,
  like stirring a pot, while the other hand taps the rhythm on a part of the head that is out of the way. At slow tempos the
  hand may make a whole circle on each beat; faster, about half that. Brushes need a head that has some roughness to grip the wires, such as
  a coated or textured one. Brush parts are seldom written out in detail; the player chooses. See also [Drum Brushes](drum-brushes.qmd).

## Rolls {#rolls}

On the snare drum there are two ways to make the sound of a roll.

- **Multiple bounce stroke** (a *buzz*, also called a press, closed or concert roll). One wrist movement makes **three or more** sounds,
  each softer than the last, five to nine being usual. Think of putting the stick on the head with a little downward weight, not
  hitting it; pressing too hard chokes the tone. A squeeze at the fulcrum, then easing the pressure once the stick has landed, makes a
  sustained buzz. Practise with each hand alone, then join them: long buzzes in each hand with a fairly slow alternation of hands
  (the roll's *primary strokes* or *skeleton*), overlapped so it sounds continuous. If the primary strokes are too fast the
  sound tightens.
- **Open double stroke** (an *open* or *rudimental* roll). One wrist movement makes **two equal** sounds. Pressure at the fulcrum just after
  the first note makes the second; you have to experiment to find the pressure that gives two, and only two, even sounds. The fingers
  pulling the stick toward the palm also help.

Rolls in a part are normally written with **slashes through the stem** (or a trill sign), whichever kind of roll you play, and the
composer seldom says which kind to use. The book's steps for reading one:

1. Decide whether the music is in a duple or triple pulse.
2. Count the slashes (including beams and flags) through the note to be rolled. That gives the rhythmic base of the roll.
3. Divide the note into that many notes (triplets if the music is triple).
4. Halve that number to get the number of hand motions (the primary strokes).
5. Play a buzz or an open double stroke on each hand motion, and finish with a single stroke. Which kind suits the music is your choice.

Example from the book: three slashes on a quarter note in 2/4 make eight thirty-second notes, so four hand motions plus the single stroke at
the end. That roll is called a **quarter-note roll**, and with open double strokes a **nine-stroke roll** (four doubles and a single).
Two slashes on an eighth note give four thirty-seconds, two hand motions and a single: an **eighth-note roll**, or with open doubles a **five-stroke
roll**. The book also describes a **long roll**, made by playing repeated multiple bounce strokes.

## Rudiments {#rudiments}

**Rudiments** are the basic rhythm patterns of the snare drum: they do for the drummer what scales, thirds and arpeggios do for a
flute or trombone player. Rudimental drumming grew in the military in the 1600s and 1700s as a way to send orders and messages to troops at
a volume they could hear, and each army had its own patterns. Charles Stewart Ashworth's *A New, Useful and Complete System of Drum
Beating* (1812) helped begin a formal list. Today there are **forty** International Drum Rudiments of the Percussive Arts Society in four families:

I. **Roll** rudiments, II. **Diddle** rudiments, III. **Flam** rudiments, IV. **Drag** rudiments.

There are many other "hybrid" rudiments from marching bands and drum corps. The book says to practise rudiments slowly at first and speed up only once the slow
tempo is mastered; eventually play each from slow to fast and back (high strokes at first, closer to the head as it speeds up), and
also at an even, moderate march tempo.

### The families

- **Rolls.** A single stroke roll is simply right, left, right, left, in even strokes. It is a rudiment, though the single stroke
  itself is not counted as a roll stroke. It is the basis of all drumming and used on timpani, mallet instruments and other
  instruments. The other rolls use the bounce or double strokes above.
- **Diddles.** The **single paradiddle** (R L R R, L R L L) is the fundamental one. It gives the alternate stickings that
  matter when music gets more technical or you play across several surfaces (timpani, concert toms, temple blocks, a kit). Both
  strokes of every double (RR or LL) must be equal in tone and strength. For speed, use the open double stroke on the doubles.
- **Flams.** A flam is a quiet **grace note** just before a louder **main note**, so it sounds like "f-LAM". It is named for the hand
  that plays the *main* note: in a **right flam** the left plays the grace; in a **left flam** the right does. Lead into it with both sticks starting
  at once, the grace-note stick a half to two inches above the head, the main stick three to ten inches: they land at slightly
  different times. Do not start both at the same height and just move the sticks at different speeds; it looks and sounds sloppy.
  With consecutive right flams the left plays the graces as taps and the right plays full strokes. With **alternating** flams the
  grace is an *up stroke* and the main note a *down stroke*, so the hands are ready for the next flam. Learn right flams, then left, then
  alternating; slowly, in a mirror if you can, as "faaa-LAM", then "fa-LAM", then "f-LAM".
- **Drags.** A drag is **two** quiet grace notes by one hand, then a stronger main note by the other. It is to the drag family what the
  flam is to flams. *Open* drag: the graces are an open double stroke, or two separate strokes at very slow tempos, but not so open that they
  stop sounding like grace notes. *Closed* drag: the graces are a multiple bounce. The book would have you hold drags back until Flams and basic rolls are secure,
  the second year for most students.
- **Ruffs.** A note with three or more grace notes: the **four-stroke ruff** is three graces and a main note, graces usually single strokes, or
  doubles when the speed or rhythm calls for it. A drag is a kind of ruff, sometimes called a three-stroke ruff.

### Rudiment player

Pick a rudiment. The staff shows the pattern as written, with the hand above each note; **R** and **L** are the right and left hands, letters in
brackets before a hand are its grace notes (a flam is **(L)R**: the left hand's grace, then the right hand's main note), and a boxed chip is an accent. Press Play and the chips light as it sounds.
Start slow.

::: {#sd-rudiments}
:::

**What this player is.** Notation and sound are made from the same table of stickings, which is checked by a script so every bar has the right number of beats.
The sticking of the single paradiddle's accents and the grace-note hands of the flam, drag and ruff are from the book. The stickings of the flam tap,
flam accent, double paradiddle, paradiddle-diddle and five-stroke roll are the common ones written from memory of the Percussive Arts Society list and have **not been checked**
against it; check them there. Note lengths are practice values (the list does not fix a speed). The grace notes and buzz are placed by the site's rules of thumb (the flam
grace about 45 ms before the main note, each further grace 45 ms earlier, buzz hits 40 ms apart and fading), not measured from a drummer. The sound is the band's sampled snare,
the same for both hands.

## Care and maintenance {#care}

1. When the drum or stand is dusty, wipe it with a soft clean cloth.
2. Put a little light household lubricant on the snare strainer when needed.
3. Tune the batter and snare heads now and then, and replace them when they are worn, dented or punctured. How is on the
   [Percussion page](percussion.qmd#heads).
4. Replace any rubber tips or insulators on the stand that are worn or missing.
5. Keep sticks in a stick bag with your other mallets and beaters. When moving the drum and stand, put them in their cases and make
   sure the **snare strainer is engaged** so the snares are not damaged.
